summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Operations and Management Area standards-track and experimental documents, to find dependencies on IPv4. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist of rules for running networks that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in operations area specs
subtitle: Surveying IPv4 dependencies in operations and management standards

tldr.problem: As networks transition from IPv4 to IPv6, management and monitoring standards must also evolve. Many SNMP and network management RFCs explicitly define IPv4 address types and assume IPv4-only addressing in network monitoring.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC systematically reviews all standards-track and experimental RFCs in the IETF Operations & Management Area, documenting IPv4 dependencies and where they appear in management protocols and information models.
tldr.outcome: The survey identifies management standards needing IPv6 updates, particularly SNMP and network monitoring specifications, providing a roadmap for management protocol evolution during IPv6 transition. Later RFCs addressed these gaps with IPv6 address types.

facts.label: IPv6 replacement RFC
facts.value: RFC 3291 (Textual Conventions for Internet Network Addresses)

today: RFC 3796 is an Informational document published in June 2004. It documents IPv4 dependencies that existed in Operations & Management standards at that time. RFC 3291 (published in 2002) and later SNMP extensions have since provided IPv6-capable replacements for the IPv4-only address types. Modern network management tools now support both IPv4 and IPv6 monitoring and configuration.

sections.title: Network Management and IPv6 Transition
sections.content:
Network operations and management require monitoring IP addresses, routing information, and network configuration. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and the MIB (Management Information Base) are central to this task. However, these standards were designed when IPv4was the only IP version, and many contain explicit definitions of IPv4-only address types.

This RFC is one of seven documents surveying IPv4 dependencies across IETF standards areas. It focuses on the Operations & Management Area, which includes SNMP, network monitoring, remote management, and the information models that describe network objects. The goal is to identify which management standards need updating to monitor and configure IPv6 networks correctly.
sections.eli5: Tools that watch over networks need to understand addresses. Many were built to only understand old-style addresses. This document finds where those tools need updating.

sections.title: Core SNMP and MIB IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
RFC 1155 (Structure of Management Information) defines the IpAddress application type as a 32-bit (4-octet) internet address, representing IPv4 only. RFC 1212 (Concise MIB definitions) specifies the same: IpAddress as four sub-identifiers in a.b.c.d notation. RFC 1213 (Management Information Base) uses this IpAddress type extensively in groups for IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, and EGP, making all these management objects IPv4-only.

RFC 2578 (SMIv2) retains the same IpAddress type (32-bit address) but marks it deprecated and notes that network addresses should be represented using TEXTUAL-CONVENTION (RFC 3291 provides IPv6-aware replacements). RFC 3416 (SNMP Protocol Operations) includes examples using IPv4 addresses from MIB2 objects. RFC 3417 (SNMP Transport Mappings) defines SnmpUDPAddress as 6 octets: 4 for IP address and 2 for UDP port, again assuming IPv4.
sections.eli5: The core SNMP rules say "an address is always four numbers". That works for IPv4 but not IPv6. Later rules marked this as old and said to use a more flexible way instead.

sections.title: Management Standards Without IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
Many Operations & Management Area standards have no IPv4 dependencies, making them already compatible with IPv6 monitoring. These include RFC 2579 (Textual Conventions for SMIv2), which does not assume IPv4; RFC 2580 (Conformance Statements for SMIv2); RFC 2819 (Remote Network Monitoring MIB); RFC 3411–3415 (the SNMP v3 architecture, message processing, applications, authentication, and access control), which are address-independent.

Notably, later SNMP standards were designed to work with any IP version because they do not embed address format assumptions. This shows that even while IPv4-dependent definitions existed, newer management frameworks could be built to support both address families.
sections.eli5: Some newer management rules don't mention addresses at all—they just say "monitor the network" without caring what format the addresses are. Those work fine with IPv6.

sections.title: IPv6 Updates for Management Standards
sections.content:
The survey recommends that standards with IPv4-specific address definitions be updated or supplemented. For SNMP, the main requirement is adding TEXTUAL-CONVENTION definitions for IPv6 addresses, as documented in RFC 3291. MIBs and management objects that currently use the 32-bit IpAddress type need updated definitions that can represent both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

Standards defining address fields in network configuration (like the DNS server address or gateway address in RFC 3017) should support both address families or become format-agnostic. The transition strategy is to define new object types for IPv6 alongside the IPv4 ones, allowing dual-stack operation during the transition period, rather than replacing IPv4 definitions immediately.
sections.eli5: The management tools need new definitions that can handle both old and new address formats. Some tools can add IPv6 versions of the same rules alongside the IPv4 ones, so both work at the same time.

sections.title: Impact and Priorities for Transition
sections.content:
The dependencies in SNMP and MIB definitions have high operational impact because network operators rely on these tools to monitor and manage the transition itself. If SNMP cannot report IPv6 addresses, network operators lose visibility into IPv6 network behavior during the transition period.

Highest priority upgrades are for the core MIB definitions (to add IPv6 address types and monitor IPv6 interfaces) and for network monitoring protocols (to observe IPv6 traffic and routing). Lower priority are updates to informational or rarely-used management extensions. The RFC emphasizes that Standards track management RFCs (which are widely deployed) should be prioritized for IPv6 awareness over Proposed or Experimental RFCs.
sections.eli5: The tools that watch the network during the transition are critical. If they can't see IPv6, nobody knows what's happening. Those are the most important to fix first.
